_meta.description: Prose content for the main About page. All numbers reference stored artifacts via validation_results.json or scoring_policy.json. Status draft = needs owner review before publishing.

about_me.text: I'm a third-year economics student at the University of Toronto with a focus in data analytics and a minor in statistics. I want to work in baseball analytics. I built this dashboard solo to develop the skills and produce the kind of work I'd want to show in that context.

purpose.text: The goal is a quick read on how a pitcher is succeeding using four independent axes: stuff, location, deception, and tunneling. The interesting part is where they disagree. A pitcher can throw a mediocre fastball to exactly the right corner at exactly the right count and outscore his underlying stuff. Another can have elite velocity and movement but give it all back by tipping sequences. Each model was validated against out-of-sample results, and bugs found along the way were fixed and documented rather than quietly patched.

model_blurbs.stuff_plus: Stuff+ (v4, promoted 2026-10-02) grades the physical shape of a pitch: velocity, movement, spin, axis differential, fastball-relative separation, and — new in v4 — horizontal approach angle residual (haa_residual), which captures how much the pitch bends laterally relative to what its release geometry predicts. It does not know where the pitch was thrown or what the count was. A 100 is league average for that season; 10 points is one standard deviation. The model is trained on 2016–2026 Statcast data (excluding 2020); every season including 2020 is scored by the single model, with 2020 values carrying an asterisk (60-game season, not in training). Knuckleballers score below average by construction, which is correct but incomplete — the model captures their unusual physics while missing why it works. Season and effective_speed features were retained from v3 (feature-drop ablations were underpowered at 30% pitcher holdout).
model_blurbs.location_plus: Location+ grades where a pitch was thrown relative to the strike zone and the count, independent of what the pitch is. It fills the deliberate gap left by Stuff+ and Tunneling+, both of which exclude plate location by design. The model was replaced in September 2026 with a five-classifier decomposed-event architecture after the original version developed a sign flip (ERA r = −0.257) and a stability collapse (year-over-year r = 0.009 for 2024→2025). The current version scores ERA r = +0.208 and xFIP r = +0.349, with the correct sign. Location measures where pitches ended up, not intent, and needs large samples for stable estimates.
model_blurbs.tunneling_plus: Tunneling+ grades how indistinguishable a pitcher's pitches look from each other at the hitter's commit point. It uses lag-context features — commit-point distance, plate-arrival distance, and shape-break between consecutive pitches — across the previous six pitches in a game. It was also replaced in September 2026 with a five-classifier decomposed-event architecture, fixing a sign flip in the prior version (ERA r = −0.218). A 2026 diagnostic found that the geometry features themselves add no independent predictive signal for real whiff rates; the model's predictive power comes from pitch-type sequencing. This is documented as an unresolved finding, not concealed. Year-over-year r² is 0.31–0.53, lower than Stuff+ as expected — sequencing is partly strategic.
model_blurbs.deception_plus: Deception+ grades pitcher body and release mechanics: arm angle, extension, release point consistency, height, and weight. It asks whether something about a pitcher's physical delivery predicts better outcomes independent of what the pitch is. The model covers 2021–2026 (arm angle was not available in Statcast before mid-2020). Year-over-year stability is the weakest of the four (r² = 0.17–0.34), likely because arm angle and release position are highly correlated (r = 0.79 leaguewide), partially proxying pitcher identity rather than delivery mechanics. Height and weight are also unresolved as possible body-type proxies. A computer-vision pipeline using broadcast video is in R&D to recover features — timing, leg lift, ball concealment — that Statcast does not publish.

items.text: All four models train toward run value (delta_run_exp) and explain very little per-pitch variance. R² values from leave-one-season-out CV are 0.0002–0.007. The models are measuring a real signal but it accounts for a small fraction of what happens on any individual pitch.

Stuff+'s out-of-sample stability (LOPO r=0.558) is substantially lower than the in-sample figure (r=0.907). The LOPO figure is the honest generalization number. The gap suggests some memorization of pitcher-season patterns even with pitcher identity excluded as a feature.

Location+ measures where pitches ended up, not intent. A missed location that happens to end up in a favorable spot scores as good command. Large samples are needed because average plate position stabilizes slowly.

Tunneling+'s geometry features (commit-point distance, plate-arrival distance, shape-break) show no independent predictive signal for real whiff rates when isolated from pitch-type sequencing information. The model predicts outcomes, but through pitch-type patterns rather than the geometric measurement it was designed around.

Deception+ covers limited seasons (2021–2026) due to arm_angle availability, and may partially recognize pitchers through correlated body-size features (arm_angle × release_pos_z r=0.79 leaguewide; height and weight included as features). Whether removing body-size features improves out-of-sample performance is unresolved.
Scores for small samples are noisy. Stuff+ uses empirical-Bayes shrinkage to handle this, but the other three models do not. A pitcher with 110 pitches has a noisier score than one with 1,500.

All four models include season as a categorical feature for era-adjustment. This means they need an annual retrain before a new season's data accumulates, or the new season falls to LightGBM's missing-category branch with uncontrolled behavior.

Stuff+ v4's validation figures are in-sample (descriptive) or from a pitcher-holdout ablation subsample (labeled 'conservative'), not true out-of-sample historical forecasts. Displayed past-season scores (2016–2026) were computed with a single model trained on all seasons 2016–2026 (excluding 2020).
2020 Stuff+ scores are based on a 60-game season and were not part of the model's training data. Treat 2020 values with caution.

Stuff+ v4 season and effective_speed ablation results were underpowered (30% pitcher holdout, 5-fold CV) — the feature-drop ablation could not distinguish dropping these features from reseeding noise. They are retained pending a more powered study.

AB (automatic ball) pitch code appears in v4 category levels but is effectively excluded by null tracking features (dropna on CORE_NUMERIC_FEATURES). One AB pitch was present in training seasons; its share in any pitcher-season is negligible (1/2247 pitches in the largest case).

items: Tunneling+ redesign: the current geometry features add no independent signal beyond pitch-type sequencing. A redesign that focuses directly on pitch-type transition patterns (rather than geometric distances) would be more honest about what the model is actually measuring.
Pitcher archetype profiles: group pitchers by arsenal shape and sequencing style rather than ranking them on a single axis. More useful for scouting context than a single score.
Pitcher-holdout test for Location+: the identifiability and memorization audit done for Stuff+ has not yet been run for Location+ or Tunneling+.

Deception+ with video-derived biomechanics: a computer-vision pipeline using broadcast video and pose tracking to recover timing, leg lift, and ball concealment features that Statcast does not publish. Currently in R&D.
Combined view: a single page showing all four scores for a pitcher side-by-side with the disagreement highlighted, so the interesting cases stand out.
A 3D tunneling viewer was developed; a working prototype exists. It is not yet integrated into the site.
